newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi seeks to import more petrol for pilgrims.
newsitem.headline: Saudi seeks to import more petrol for pilgrims.

text.p: Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer and exporter, is aiming to import more petrol to meet the demands of two million Moslems at next month's annual pilgrimage in the kingdom, Gulf-based traders said on Monday.
State-owned Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company in terms of reserves, has issued a tender to buy 1.5 million barrels of petrol for delivery in April, traders said.
"They probably need the barrels because of the haj (pilgrimage)...it's building up inventory to prevent possible shortfalls," said one Saudi-based Asian oil executive.

The haj usually increases road traffic for the one million Saudis travelling to the holy cities of Mecca and Medina and another million foreign pilgrims, many of whom arrive at the commercial capital Jeddah with special haj visas.
Mecca, one of Islam's holiest sites, is 72 km (45 miles) southeast of Jeddah, the main port of entry for most pilgrims.
Medina is 414 km (257 miles) northeast of Jeddah.

Although the Saudis have tendered for 1.5 million barrels of petrol, the actual volume that Aramco would buy through the tender was still unclear and some traders said that current strong market prices might lead the state oil firm to delay or cut back on tender purchases.
Aramco regularly imports petrol from neighbouring Bahrain under a term contract and has also bought the occasional cargo from the spot market to cover shortfalls, traders said.
A need for more sophisticated upgrading units at its refineries and export allocations to foreign joint venture refinery partners in the kingdom limit Saudi petrol output.

Traders said Aramco's tender, which could cost it about $45 million at current market prices, was a sign that even local production from the kingdom's eight refineries and current import levels could not satisfy rising demand in Saudi Arabia, where prices at the pump are 16 cents a litre (0.2 gallon).
"Aramco has been buying spot (petrol) cargoes since the end of 1996 but this is its biggest tender to date," a Kuwait-based trader said.
Aramco's tender requests that it be supplied at the eastern port city of Ras Tanura where a major refinery is under repair.
Ras Tanura refinery was badly damaged in a 1990 fire as it was gearing up to supply fuel to allied forces assembling for the 1991 Gulf War.
The partial loss of capacity at Ras Tanura increased fuel reliance on refineries in western Saudi Arabia.
Saudi petrol demand is centred in the capital Riyadh and the populous Eastern Province but most of its petrol is produced at refineries on its western Red Sea coast, traders said.
"There is an east-west imbalance. Products from Yanbu and Rabigh have to be sent all the way to the east," an oil industry executive based in the Gulf said.
With the haj boosting petrol use in the kingdom, the Ras Tanura tender would enable the western refineries to concentrate mainly on meeting Red Sea coast demand, traders said.
Saudi domestic petrol output was also being crimped by higher exports of naphtha which is used as a petrochemical feedstock and can be converted into petrol, traders said.
Naphtha prices have outperformed most other petroleum product prices this year.
